steps.explanationAfterStep: The 'butterfly' transition state: both C–C bonds form on the same face of the alkene as the iodide moves to zinc, so the reaction is stereospecific (a cis-alkene gives a cis-cyclopropane). Zinc also binds nearby oxygen atoms, so an allylic OH directs the CH₂ to its own face. The app does not check stereochemistry yet.

title: Simmons–Smith cyclopropanation
subtitle: A zinc carbenoid adds CH₂ to cyclohexene in one step
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 38

reactants.caption: the Simmons–Smith reagent (iodomethylzinc iodide) + cyclohexene
hintTiers: The CH₂ carries both a leaving group (iodide) and a C–Zn bond: it behaves like a carbene without ever being free (a carbenoid). Three arrows, all at once.
The alkene π pair bonds to the CH₂ carbon; the C–Zn bonding pair bonds the CH₂ to the other alkene carbon; the iodine moves from carbon to zinc.
C=C π bond → new bond from one alkene carbon to CH₂; C–Zn bond → new bond from CH₂ to the other alkene carbon; C–I bond → new I–Zn bond.
reactants.learnerPrompt: The CH₂ is delivered to the alkene in one step.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Losing iodide would need a free CH₂ carbene, which is far too reactive and would not be stereospecific or selective. Zinc holds on to the iodide as the CH₂ is passed to the alkene.
The alkene bonds to the CH₂ carbon, not to zinc.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right: both C–C bonds form. The CH₂ carbon would now have five bonds: the C–I bond breaks as iodine moves to zinc.

mechanismSummary: Zinc (activated with copper) inserts into a C–I bond of diiodomethane to give ICH₂ZnI; this insertion is not drawn, because the app has no steps for metal insertion. The reagent is a carbenoid: it transfers CH₂ to the alkene in one concerted step, with iodide moving to zinc, so no free carbene forms and the alkene geometry is kept. Et₂Zn with CH₂I₂ (the Furukawa modification) gives a similar reagent.
